subtitle: A Jain Voice in the Shaivite Thunder of Malwa

panels.shot: epic three-quarter view, low-angle wide of a crowded court with banners and stone pillars, Dhanapala in foreground holding a palm-leaf manuscript, Shaivite king dimly seen on throne
panels.action: Dhanapala stands calm yet intent in a grand stone hall, palm-leaf manuscript held close, as robed Shaivite courtiers and Brahmin scholars cluster around a distant throne under hanging bells and carved tridents.

dialogue.text: In a Shaivite court of Malwa where hymns to Shiva filled the air, a Jain scholar named Dhanapala wrote, debated, and survived—leaving us a novel that reveals how many voices a single throne could hold.

i18n.hi: मालवा के शैव दरबार में, जहाँ शिव-स्तोत्र गूँजते थे, जैन पंडित धनपाल लिखते, बहस करते, बचते रहे—और एक कथा छोड़ गए जो दिखाती है, एक सिंहासन पर कितनी आवाज़ें बैठ सकती हैं।

panels.shot: slow push-in on a palm-leaf manuscript in lamplight, with a faint reflection of Dhanapala’s face in a polished copper water pot nearby
panels.action: In a dim study lit by an oil lamp, a palm-leaf manuscript lies open beside an ink stylus, while Dhanapala’s thoughtful face, bearded and serene, hovers in reflection on a copper pot of water.

dialogue.text: Before we see the court, we must meet the witness. The Jain writer Dhanapala, around the turn of the first millennium, took up his stylus and began to describe the world that whirled around him.

i18n.hi: दरबार से पहले, गवाह से मिलें। पहली सहस्राब्दी के मोड़ पर, जैन लेखक धनपाल ने लेखनी उठाई और अपने चारों तरफ घूमती दुनिया को शब्दों में पकड़ना शुरू किया।

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder close-up of Dhanapala writing on a leaf, the words hinted but not legible, with a window showing a distant city skyline of Dhara
panels.action: Seen from behind, Dhanapala bends over a fresh palm leaf, stylus poised, while through a latticed window the outlines of Dhara’s temples, markets and a hill-fort rise against the afternoon haze.

dialogue.text: He lived in Malwa, under the Paramaras, where kings like Vakpati Munja and Bhoja ruled from Dhara. In his lexicon’s preface, Dhanapala quietly notes a victory at Manyakheta—an historian’s gold hidden in a grammarian’s aside.

i18n.hi: वह मालवा में परमारों के अधीन रहते थे, जब वाक्पति मुँज और भोज जैसे राजा धारा से राज करते थे। अपने कोश की भूमिका में धनपाल चुपचाप मण्यखेता की विजय का ज़िक्र कर जाते हैं—इतिहास का खज़ाना, व्याकरण की पंक्ति में छुपा।

panels.shot: wide bird’s-eye view over an army on the march across the Narmada plain, banners fluttering, with a caption-like composition suggesting distance and scale
panels.action: An army snakes across a dusty plain, elephant lines lumbering, horse columns kicking up clouds, as banners with the Paramara emblem sway in the heat under a wide, pale sky.

dialogue.text: That aside recalls the day Siyaka, Munja’s predecessor, struck at the Rashtrakuta capital of Manyakheta. The city of an old empire fell to a rising house from Malwa, and the balance of the Deccan shifted.

i18n.hi: वह एक पंक्ति हमें उस दिन पर ले जाती है जब मुँज के पूर्वज Siyaka ने राष्ट्रकूट राजधानी मण्यखेता पर वार किया। एक पुराना साम्राज्य गिरा, मालवा का नया घर उभरा, और दक्खिन का पलड़ा बदल गया।

panels.shot: medium wide of Manyakheta’s skyline with temples and palaces as distant fires and smoke rise, seen from outside the city walls
panels.action: From a low ridge outside Manyakheta, we see its clustered temples and palace towers, some roofs wreathed in smoke, as streams of people hurry out through the city gate under the watch of armed riders.

dialogue.text: Dhanapala’s preface to the Paiyalacchi-namamala preserves this notice of Siyaka’s feat. It anchors his life to real campaigns, real dates, and shows how a Jain scholar watched kings remake the map, leaf in hand.

i18n.hi: धनपाल की Paiyalacchi-namamala की भूमिका में Siyaka की इस जीत की खबर ज्यों की त्यों बची है। इससे उनका जीवन असली सेनाओं, असली तारीख़ों से जुड़ता है, और दिखाता है कि एक जैन पंडित कैसे राजाओं को नक्शा बदलते देखता रहा, हाथ में पांडुलिपि लेकर।

panels.shot: low-angle interior wide of Munja’s court, with Munja on a lion-legged throne blurred in background, Dhanapala among other scholars in foreground
panels.action: Under high stone arches carved with lotuses, Munja sits on a lion-footed throne while Brahmin pundits and ascetics crowd the hall; to one side, Dhanapala stands modestly with a bundle of manuscripts, watching sharply.

dialogue.text: Under Vakpati Munja, the Paramara court of Dhara became a gathering place for poets and philosophers. Among them, tradition places Dhanapala, serving a ruler devoted to Shiva yet hungry for many kinds of learning.

i18n.hi: वाक्पति मुँज के नीचे, धारा का परमार दरबार कवियों और दार्शनिकों की सभा बन गया। परंपरा कहती है, इन्हीं में धनपाल भी थे—एक ऐसे राजा की सेवा में, जो शिवभक्त था, पर हर तरह के ज्ञान का भूखा।

panels.shot: tight profile close-up of Dhanapala in the court, eyes intent, as brahmin scholar hands point and argue in the blurred background
panels.action: In sharp profile, Dhanapala listens, lips slightly parted, while in the soft focus behind him Brahmin scholars gesture animatedly, palms raised in debate, their prayer threads and tufted hair visible.

dialogue.text: The court was Shaivite in ritual, with Brahmin officiants and Vedic recitations. But its halls resounded also with Jain logic, Buddhist memories, and regional tongues. Dhanapala’s presence itself is a record of that plural sound.

i18n.hi: रसम-रिवाज़ में दरबार शैव था—ब्राह्मण पुरोहित, वैदिक पाठ। पर इन्हीं दीवारों में जैन तर्क, बौद्ध स्मृतियाँ और देशी बोलियाँ भी गूँजती थीं। खुद धनपाल की मौजूदगी इस बहसुर ध्वनि का जीता-जागता सबूत है।

panels.shot: medium shot of Dhanapala presenting a manuscript to Munja on the dais, other scholars watching with mixed expressions
panels.action: Standing at the foot of the dais, Dhanapala offers a neatly tied palm-leaf manuscript with both hands, head bowed slightly, as Munja leans forward with interest and a few older Brahmin scholars glance sideways, weighing this non-Vedic text.

dialogue.speaker: dhanapala
dialogue.text: My lord, words can be another kind of campaign.

i18n.hi: महाराज, शब्द भी एक तरह की युद्ध-चढ़ाई हैं।

panels.shot: transition shot, dissolve feel, where Munja’s figure fades and Bhoja’s figure sharpens on the same throne
panels.action: The same throne scene is shown twice in one frame: Munja’s form, slightly transparent, overlapped by the firmer, younger figure of Bhoja taking his place, while Dhanapala remains in the same spot, a constant in the changing court.

dialogue.text: After Munja, his nephew Bhoja rose to the throne, around 1010 CE. In Bhoja’s long reign, the Paramara court became a legend of learning, and Dhanapala’s career bridged these two rulers, Jain under Shaivite patronage.

i18n.hi: मुँज के बाद, उनके भतीजे भोज ने लगभग 1010 ई. के आस-पास गद्दी सँभाली। भोज के लंबे राज में परमार दरबार विद्या की कथा बन गया, और धनपाल का जीवन इन दो राजाओं के बीच पुल बना—जैन, पर शैव आश्रय में।

panels.shot: sweeping wide of Bhoja’s court in full session, with multiple scholars of different dress, merchants and envoys present, Dhanapala seated among writers
panels.action: In a bustling audience hall, Bhoja sits in state, while rows of scholars in varied robes, traders in rich garments, and foreign envoys stand in ordered clusters; Dhanapala is seated cross-legged near a pillar, writing even as he listens.

dialogue.text: Later storytellers made Bhoja a near-mythical patron of all arts. In the record, too, inscriptions show him as a Shaivite king. Yet Jain authors like Dhanapala flourished in his orbit, their works copied and cherished.

i18n.hi: बाद की कहानियों ने भोज को हर कला के लगभग पौराणिक संरक्षक में बदल दिया। अभिलेखों में भी वह शैव राजा दिखते हैं। फिर भी धनपाल जैसे जैन लेखक उनके घेरे में फले-फूले—उनकी रचनाएँ नकल हुईं, सँभाली गईं।

panels.shot: medium interior shot of a Jain temple at Bhojpur under construction, with sculptors at work and Dhanapala visiting with a monk
panels.action: Beside a rocky hillside, the stone walls of a Jain shrine rise, masons chiselling images as a Jain monk in white speaks to Dhanapala, who gazes up at the unfinished doorway with quiet satisfaction.

dialogue.text: At Bhojpur, not far from Bhoja’s great unfinished Shiva temple, stands evidence of a Jain shrine. Its stones confirm, silently, that Jain communities and patrons, too, had a place in Bhoja’s domain.

i18n.hi: भोज के अधूरे महाशिव मंदिर से ज़्यादा दूर नहीं, भोजपुर में एक जैन मंदिर के निशान मिलते हैं। ये पत्थर चुपचाप बताते हैं कि भोज के राज्य में जैन समाज और दानदाता भी अपनी जगह रखते थे।

panels.shot: intimate medium shot of Dhanapala seated in a Jain upashraya with monks and laypersons, discussing a text
panels.action: In a simple hall with plain pillars, Dhanapala sits on a low platform, palm-leaf in hand, while Jain monks and lay devotees sit around him, listening as he gestures gently to explain a lexical point.

dialogue.text: Within Jain spaces, Dhanapala composed for his own community. The Paiyalacchi-namamala, a Prakrit lexicon, shows him working between languages, between court Sanskrit and Jain speech, between royal notice and monastic need.

i18n.hi: जैन विहारों के भीतर, धनपाल ने अपनी ही सभा के लिए लिखा। Paiyalacchi-namamala, एक प्राकृत कोश, उन्हें भाषाओं के बीच काम करते दिखाता है—दरबारी संस्कृत और जैन बोली के बीच, राज-उल्लेख और मठ की ज़रूरत के बीच।

panels.shot: dramatic low-angle of Dhanapala reading aloud in court, courtiers leaning in, with the sense of performing a story
panels.action: Back in the royal hall, Dhanapala stands upright, palm-leaf held up as if reciting, his voice imagined ringing through the pillars, while courtiers sit forward, some smiling, some frowning, drawn into the unseen tale.

dialogue.text: His Tilaka-Manjari, a Sanskrit prose romance, reveals the world he knew. It is not a dry grammar, but a long, crafted story—where love, politics, merchants, monks and seasons all share the same pages.

i18n.hi: उनकी Tilaka-Manjari, संस्कृत गद्य-रूप कथा, उनके देखे हुए संसार को खोलती है। यह सूखी व्याकरण नहीं, एक लंबी तराशी हुई कहानी है—जहाँ प्रेम, राजनीति, व्यापारी, भिक्षु और ऋतु—all एक ही पन्नों पर साथ चलते हैं।

panels.shot: montage-like wide panel divided subtly into four scenes: courtly scene, bustling city bazaar, merchant caravan, ascetics on forest path
panels.action: A single wide frame holds four vignettes: a glittering court scene; a crowded city market with fabric sellers; a merchant caravan crossing a river on boats; and a pair of ascetics walking through sparse woodland under cloudy skies.

dialogue.text: Within that tale, we glimpse royal intrigue in palace halls, crowded city streets, caravans of traders, and ascetics on the road. Tilaka-Manjari serves as a window into the social fabric of Malwa and its neighbors around 1000 CE.

i18n.hi: उस कथा में हम महलों की साज़िशें, भीड़भरी गलियाँ, व्यापारियों के कारवाँ और सड़क के साधुओं की झलक पकड़ते हैं। Tilaka-Manjari मालवा और उसके आस-पास के समाज का हज़ार ई. के दौर का झरोखा बन जाती है।

panels.shot: medium shot of a merchant counting coins in a shop, with a ledger and an image of a deity in the background
panels.action: Inside a wooden-fronted shop, a merchant sits cross-legged, counting coins onto a cloth while a ledger lies open beside him and a small image of a deity watches from a wall niche above.

dialogue.text: The narrative lingers on merchants and contracts, on gifts and dowries. It shows how wealth moved alongside piety, how guilds, donors, and bankers stood just behind the dazzling front of kings and priests.

i18n.hi: कहानी व्यापारियों और सौदों, दान और दहेज पर ठहरती है। यह दिखाती है कि धन के धागे भक्ति के साथ-साथ कैसे चलते थे—गिल्ड, दाता और साहूकार, राजाओं और पुरोहितों की चमक के ठीक पीछे खड़े।

panels.shot: medium long shot of Jain and non-Jain ascetics conversing at a crossroads under a tree
panels.action: Beneath a spreading tree at a dusty crossroads, a Jain monk in white, a matted-haired Shaivite ascetic, and a travelling bard stand in conversation, their different garments and emblems marking their paths.

dialogue.text: Dhanapala’s pages also carry Jain mendicants, Brahmin ritualists, and other wanderers. Their meetings at crossroads hint at the debates and exchanges that must have flowed in and around Bhoja’s Shaivite court.

i18n.hi: धनपाल के पन्नों पर जैन साधु, ब्राह्मण कर्ता, और दूसरे यायावर भी चलते हैं। चौराहों पर उनकी मुलाकातें उन वाद-विवादों का आभास देती हैं जो भोज के शैव दरबार के अंदर-बाहर बहते होंगे।

panels.shot: somber close-up of Dhanapala’s hand writing the preface line that mentions Manyakheta, with his face barely visible at frame edge
panels.action: The image focuses on Dhanapala’s hand as he etches a line onto the palm leaf, his fingers steady, while the shadow of his face falls across the script, suggesting care in recording this detail.

dialogue.text: By inserting Siyaka’s Manyakheta victory into a lexicon’s preface, he anchors a literary work in hard political fact. His choice tells us that for him, words and power, narrative and conquest, were always intertwined.

i18n.hi: सियक की मण्यखेता विजय को कोश की भूमिका में डालकर, वह साहित्यिक रचना को ठोस राजनीति से बाँध देते हैं। उनकी यह चाल बताती है कि उनके लिए शब्द और सत्ता, कथा और विजय—हमेशा आपस में गुंथे थे।

panels.shot: pattern interrupt: side-by-side images, on left a colourful later manuscript painting of Dhanapala and Bhoja, on right a stark inscriptional stone of Bhoja with Shaivite symbol
panels.action: On one side, a stylized painting shows Dhanapala and Bhoja in imagined intimacy; on the other, a rough stone inscription slab with a clear trident emblem stands alone, while Dhanapala in the middle looks toward both, contemplative.

dialogue.text: Later prabandha tales claimed Dhanapala converted Bhoja to Jainism or humbled Vedic rites. Inscriptions, however, show Bhoja firmly Shaivite. The contrast reveals how later sectarian hopes reshaped memories of this shared court.

i18n.hi: बाद के प्रबंधों ने दावा किया कि धनपाल ने भोज को जैन बना लिया या वैदिक यज्ञों को झुका दिया। अभिलेख, हालांकि, भोज को पक्के शैव दिखाते हैं। यह फ़र्क बताता है कि बाद की साम्प्रदायिक इच्छाएँ किस तरह इस साझा दरबार की याद बदल ले गईं।

panels.shot: wide shot of Dhanapala walking between two buildings—on one side a Shaivite temple, on the other a Jain shrine—with evening light stretching his shadow
panels.action: At dusk, Dhanapala walks along a stone path, a manuscript under his arm; to his left rises a tall Shaivite temple tower, to his right the plainer front of a Jain shrine, his long shadow touching both thresholds.

dialogue.text: The more we follow him, the less his life looks like a conversion drama and the more it appears as a practice of crossing thresholds—moving between Jain and Shaivite spaces while holding to his own path.

i18n.hi: जितना हम उन्हें पकड़ने की कोशिश करते हैं, उनका जीवन किसी ‘धर्म-परिवर्तन नाटक’ से कम, और दहलीज़ पार करने की साध practice से ज़्यादा दिखता है—जैन और शैव दोनों जगहों से गुजरते हुए, अपनी ही राह पर टिके।

panels.shot: introspective close-up of older Dhanapala, lines on his face, looking down at stacked manuscripts
panels.action: Now older, with fine lines around his eyes, Dhanapala gazes softly at a neat stack of his manuscripts, fingers resting lightly on the top leaf as if taking leave or blessing them.

dialogue.text: We do not know how Dhanapala’s life ended, or whether his position always felt secure. But his texts survived copying and time, passing through hands that cared more about their words than their author’s sect.

i18n.hi: हम नहीं जानते धनपाल का अंत कैसे हुआ, या उनकी कुर्सी हमेशा सुरक्षित लगी या नहीं। पर उनकी रचनाएँ नकल, पाठ और समय के पार बचीं—ऐसे हाथों से गुजरती हुई जो उनके मजहब से ज़्यादा, उनके शब्दों की परवाह करते थे।

panels.shot: final contemplative wide shot of a modern scholar in a library reading a manuscript, with a faint superimposed image of Dhanapala behind
panels.action: In a modern archive room lined with shelves, a present-day scholar bends over a manuscript on a desk, while a faint, translucent figure of Dhanapala seems to stand behind, watching quietly over his own words.

dialogue.text: Today, when we open Tilaka-Manjari or the Paiyalacchi-namamala, we hear not a single king’s voice, but a layered conversation across faiths; Dhanapala’s Jain prose in a Shaivite court shows that a court’s greatness is measured by how many languages it lets truth speak.

i18n.hi: आज जब हम Tilaka-Manjari या Paiyalacchi-namamala खोलते हैं, तो हमें किसी एक राजा की नहीं, परत-दर-परत चलती कई आस्थाओं की बातचीत सुनाई देती है; शैव दरबार में जैन धनपाल की गद्य-आवाज़ दिखाती है कि दरबार की महत्ता इस पर है कि वह सच को कितनी भाषाओं में बोलने दे।

subtitle_i18n.en: A Jain Voice in the Shaivite Thunder of Malwa
subtitle_i18n.hi: मालवा के शैव गड़गड़ाहट में एक जैन स्वर
